To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the steroid hormone receptors in breast cancer are not only a prognostic indicator but also provide the basis for endocrine therapy; 2) the endocrine tumour of the GEP-system is a heterogeneous entity which should be classified according to its hormone production pattern; 3) the peptide hormone production of non-neuroendocrinal neoplasms is an intriguing phenomenon which sheds some new light on histogenesis and embryological origin of these neoplasma.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

peptide hormone production by endocrine tumour cells is not a rare phenomenon but is a common event, which is often clinically silent and therefore of limited diagnostic value, whereas peptide hormone production by non-neuro-endocrine tumours is a rare event and is of diagnostic value in the search for a primary neoplasm.
peptide hormone producing cells are not restricted to endocrine tumours but are found also in non-endocrine tumours.
peptide hormones can be demonstrated by immunocytochemical methods in a variety of neoplasms, but that the clinical relevance of these findings is still limited.
The main takeaway from our work is that
peptide hormone production in carcinoma can be a valuable diagnostic marker and that it can also be a useful prognostic factor.
the presence of hormone producing cells in non-endocrine neoplasma is not an exceptional phenomenon but rather the rule, at least in the GEP system.
peptide hormone production in endocrine and non-endocrine tumors is not an uncommon phenomenon and is probably a more frequent event than previously assumed.
